articles.title: Number of suspected Ebola cases in DR Congo passes 900 as health workers face attacks and shortages | Ebola | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: Congolese authorities reported 904 suspected Ebola cases and 119 deaths, with the outbreak posing a "very high" risk for the country. The World Health Organization stated that the global spread of the disease remains low.  Health challenges include arson attacks on Ebola treatment centers and strict burial protocols, which have led to anger from local communities. The outbreak is occurring in a region plagued by violence and displacement, exacerbated by international aid cuts, making it difficult for health authorities to contain the virus.

articles.title: Andhra Pradesh govt. steps up Ebola preparedness, plans passenger screening at airports - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Andhra Pradesh's government announced precautionary measures in response to global concerns over the Ebola virus, including disease surveillance at international airports and isolation wards in hospitals.  The announcement follows a travel advisory issued by the Union government, urging citizens to avoid non-essential travel to three African countries affected by the virus: the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan.

articles.title: Mayday! SA scientists identified hantavirus outbreak in 24 hours - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: Lucille Blumberg, a South African infectious disease specialist, and her colleagues at the National Institute for Communicable Diseases were alerted to an outbreak aboard the Dutch cruise ship MV Hondius.  After ruling out other potential causes like Legionella or bird flu, they determined that the passenger's illness was caused by hantavirus, a rare rodent-borne virus found in South America. The team received assistance from WHO, the UN health agency, and experts from South America and the United States to confirm the diagnosis.

articles.title: Govt toughens airport screening amid Ebola outbreak - Newspaper - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: Pakistan's health ministry has intensified screening measures at airports and directed all provinces to remain on alert following the recent Ebola outbreak in Africa.  The WHO upgraded the risk assessment for the disease, but did not advise any travel restrictions. The Red Cross announced three volunteer deaths in the DRC, while Uganda confirmed three new cases of the virus, bringing the total to five. The African Union's health agency warned that 10 countries are at risk of being affected by the Ebola virus.

articles.title: BMCRI working on setting up a centralised diagnostic hub to ease burden on Victoria Hospital’s Infosys central laboratory - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI) is proposing to centralize its laboratory services, including the Infosys Foundation lab, to address increasing patient load and delays in test results. The plan involves consolidating five other labs under one roof on the top floor of the outpatient department building, streamlining sample collection, and providing digital access to reports.  The project aims to improve efficiency, reduce overcrowding, and enhance quality control while addressing staffing shortages and infrastructure limitations.

articles.title: Nursing student dies during surgery at Tiruchi government hospital; colleagues stage protest - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: A third-year nursing student at the K.A.P. Viswanatham Government Medical College in Tiruchi, Seethalakshmi, died after suffering a cardiac arrest during surgery at the Mahatma Gandhi Memorial Government Hospital on Saturday (May 23, 2026).  The incident sparked protests by over 300 nursing students who alleged medical negligence. A high-level inquiry committee has been formed to investigate the "adverse medical event." The committee will be led by N. Basker, medical superintendent of the Rajiv Gandhi Government General Hospital. Tamil Nadu BJP president, Nainar Nagendran, demanded a compensation of ₹25 lakh for the student's family and criticized the government's handling of healthcare in the state.

articles.title: Red Cross volunteers die from suspected Ebola in DR Congo
articles.rephrased_article: Three Red Cross volunteers have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo from suspected Ebola, likely contracted while working with deceased individuals. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said the volunteers were working in the eastern region of Ituri on a project unrelated to the virus before it was identified.  The outbreak has resulted in over 170 suspected deaths and 750 suspected cases, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to raise the public health risk from "high" to "very high". The outbreak involves a rare species of Ebola known as Bundibugyo, which poses a significant threat due to its lack of proven vaccine.

articles.title: More than 500 children die in measles outbreak in Bangladesh | Health News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: Over 500 children have died in Bangladesh from a measles outbreak, the deadliest surge in decades. The Bangladesh health department reports the death toll has reached 512 since March 15th, with most cases occurring among children aged six months to five years old.  The United Nations Children's Agency (UNICEF) is working on a mass vaccination campaign that has reached 18 million children, but experts warn that gaps in immunizations could worsen antimicrobial resistance.

articles.title: ‘Every health facility said they were full’: alarm over rapid spread of Ebola in DRC | Ebola | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and Mercy Corps have warned that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is spreading rapidly, overwhelming healthcare systems. The virus has claimed nearly 180 lives since its emergence in April, and hospitals are struggling to cope with the influx of suspected cases.  The spread of the disease is exacerbated by cultural practices like funeral wakes, which can facilitate transmission. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) reports that healthcare facilities are overwhelmed, and there is a shortage of isolation wards.

articles.title: Meet discusses emerging trends in cardiovascular interventions - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: The annual Society of Invasive Cardiovascular Professionals (SICP) conference, SICPCON 2026, began in [Location] on Saturday.  SICP President Johnson P.J. emphasized the importance of continuous scientific training and collaboration for safer cardiac procedures. The two-day event features expert-led sessions on various topics including complex coronary interventions, imaging-guided angioplasty, and emerging device technologies. SICP Organising Secretary Jayapalan M.P. highlighted the focus on practical learning, multidisciplinary coordination, and patient safety in invasive cardiac procedures.

articles.title: Toddler recovers after month-long critical care battle at Bengaluru hospital following road accident - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: A one-year-nine-month-old child, Vihaan S. Jithin, suffered severe brain and lung injuries following a road accident in Bengaluru.  Doctors at Manipal Hospital Yelahanka treated the child for nearly a month, addressing multiple life-threatening complications including multidrug-resistant infection, aspiration-related lung injury, and neurological damage. The doctors used a combination of mechanical ventilation, bronchoscopy, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and rehabilitation to help Vihaan regain breathing, eating, and walking abilities.  The child was eventually discharged after 30 days in intensive care.

articles.title: Uganda confirms three new Ebola cases, bringing total to five | Ebola News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: Uganda's Ministry of Health confirmed three new Ebola cases, bringing the total number of infections to five. The new cases include a driver who transported the country’s first confirmed patient and a health worker exposed while caring for that patient.  The WHO has revised its risk assessment for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola to "very high" at the national level, "high" at the regional level, and "low" at the global level. The outbreak is centered in Democratic Republic of the Congo, where nearly 750 suspected cases and 177 suspected deaths have been recorded.  The WHO is working with partners to contain the outbreak and support affected people.

articles.title: Experts urge hydration, awareness to prevent heat-related illnesses - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Experts at a webinar organized by The Hindu warned against delaying water consumption during extreme summer conditions, as symptoms like dizziness and excessive sweating can indicate serious heat-related illnesses.  Dr. Jaichitra Suresh, senior consultant physician and diabetologist at Soukya Clinic and Home Healthcare, and Dr. Karthik Gunasekaran, professor in the Department of General Medicine at Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore, discussed the impact of rising temperatures on public health. They emphasized staying hydrated, avoiding direct sunlight during peak hours, wearing light-colored clothing, and reducing strenuous activity to prevent heat-related illnesses.

articles.title: Uganda confirms 3 new Ebola cases as WHO warns against underestimating outbreak risk - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: Uganda's health ministry confirmed three new Ebola cases, bringing the total to five in the country. The new infections include a driver and a health worker who were exposed to the first confirmed patient, as well as a woman from the Democratic Republic of Congo who entered Uganda with symptoms.  The World Health Organization (WHO) has declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern due to its potential for spreading beyond Congo and Uganda. The WHO Africa director warned against underestimating the outbreak's severity, emphasizing the lack of a vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain.

articles.title: Inquiry panel at Multan hospital finds 9 doctors, officials at fault for surgery conducted sans HIV screening - Pakistan - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: Nishtar Medical University has found nine doctors and hospital officials guilty of misconduct and violation of screening protocols in a case involving surgery on an HIV-positive patient, prompting disciplinary action by the Punjab government.  The inquiry committee recommended disciplinary proceedings under the Punjab Employees Efficiency, Discipline and Accountability (Peeda) Act 2006. The Punjab health department suspended several officials, including Dr Fariha Ahmed, Rida Zahra, and others for incompetence and mismanagement.  The incident has raised concerns about compliance with infection-control protocols at the hospital.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak: 'Speed, money and compassion' - lessons from a survivor and other experts
articles.rephrased_article: The Democratic Republic of Congo is grappling with a new Ebola outbreak, prompting comparisons to the devastating 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic.  Patrick Faley, an Ebola survivor from Liberia, recalls the horrors of that crisis and warns against complacency. He emphasizes the importance of community trust, safe burials, and clear communication in controlling outbreaks. Dr. Patrick Otim, the WHO's area manager for Africa, stresses the need for swift action, emphasizing early detection and isolation as crucial to containing transmission.  Professor Thomas Geisbert, a leading Ebola expert, highlights the lack of an effective vaccine for Bundibugyo, a rare strain of the virus, while urging investment in research and development. The WHO is prioritizing the use of experimental anti-viral drug Obladesivir, but experts warn that containment efforts must be swift to prevent further spread.

articles.title: Ebola virus: surveillance, screening stepped up at Kochi airport - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Cochin International Airport Limited (CIAL) and the Airport Health Organisation (APHO) held an emergency preparedness meeting to address the global Ebola outbreak.  The meeting resulted in intensified health surveillance and precautionary protocols at the airport, including strengthened passenger monitoring systems for early symptom detection and coordinated public health response measures.

articles.title: KARD, Khandre condemn assault on BRIMS resident doctor - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: The Karnataka Association of Resident Doctors (KARD) and Bidar district in-charge Minister Eshwar B. Khandre condemned the alleged assault of a resident doctor at Bidar Institute of Medical Sciences (BRIMS), urging the state government to improve security for doctors working in public hospitals.  A letter sent to the Director of Medical Education on Friday stated that Tukaram, a 28-year-old orthopaedic resident doctor, was allegedly assaulted while attending to an injured patient in the casualty ward around 1 a.m. on Friday.

articles.title: ‘It would be a big mistake’: WHO Africa chief warns against underestimating Ebola virus risk in Congo, Uganda - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organization's Africa director, Mohamed Yakub Janabi, warned against underestimating the risk of the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and neighboring Uganda.  He stated that a single case could trigger wider transmission, emphasizing the need for increased attention to the outbreak due to the lack of a vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain. Janabi urged international cooperation to control the outbreak, highlighting the difficulty in assessing its duration due to the "hyperdynamic movement of people."  Efforts are underway to increase testing, strengthen infection prevention measures, and improve community engagement.

articles.title: Ebola risk now at highest level in DR Congo, says WHO - World - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organisation (WHO) has raised the risk assessment level for the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo to very high, citing a rapidly spreading epidemic with nearly 750 suspected cases and 177 suspected deaths.  Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO chief, emphasized the urgency of containing the virus, particularly due to violence and insecurity hindering response efforts. While Uganda's situation is stable, WHO has deployed international staff and prioritized existing treatments like monoclonal antibodies and olibdesivir for clinical trials.

articles.title: WHO says 12th person infected with hantavirus detected in the Netherlands | Health News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organization (WHO) confirmed a 12th hantavirus case in the Netherlands, involving a Dutch crew member on the MV Hondius cruise ship.  Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO chief, urged countries to continue monitoring passengers and cautioned against further spread. The infected crew member is isolated at a hospital while over 600 contacts are being monitored in 30 countries. The Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) stated that the chance of further spread remains low.

articles.title: Renowned infectious diseases expert Dr Naseem Salahuddin passes away - Pakistan - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: Dr. Naseem Salahuddin, a renowned infectious diseases expert and professor emeritus at Indus Hospital, passed away on Friday.  The hospital expressed its sorrow over her passing, noting her dedication to patient care, medical education, and humanitarian service. Dr. Salahuddin was a member of the World Health Organization’s Expert Advisory Panel on Rabies since 2004 and played a pivotal role in raising awareness about rabies prevention and treatment. She also authored books and contributed to various scholarly journals and news outlets including Dawn.

articles.title: Suspected Ebola cases triple in a week as WHO warns of rapid spread in DRC | Global development | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organization (WHO) has revised its threat assessment for the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo to "very high," citing a rapid spread and increasing number of suspected cases. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, is concentrated in Ituri province with some cases reported elsewhere in the country and neighboring Uganda. Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO director-general, highlighted the need to address distrust among local communities for successful response efforts while acknowledging a "good sign" of improved detection rates.  Despite these challenges, Dr Anne Ancia, WHO representative in the DRC, remains optimistic about containing the outbreak.

articles.title: UK scientists developing Ebola vaccine that could be ready for trials in months
articles.rephrased_article: Oxford University scientists are developing a new Ebola vaccine using the same technology employed during the COVID-19 pandemic. The experimental vaccine, which uses a modified chimpanzee cold virus to deliver genetic material about the Bundibugyo species of Ebola virus, could be ready for clinical trials in two to three months. The World Health Organization (WHO) has upgraded the risk level from "high" to "very high" in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak is centered. The vaccine will likely be used through ring vaccination, targeting those most at risk of infection and close contacts of infected individuals.

articles.title: Ebola risk raised to 'very high' in DR Congo
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organization (WHO) has raised the Ebola risk in the Democratic Republic of Congo to "very high" due to the outbreak's rapid spread and fatality rate.  Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO head, stated that while the risk is high in the region and globally, it remains low at a global level. The outbreak has resulted in 177 suspected deaths and 750 suspected cases so far, with no proven vaccine for the rare Bundibugyo strain.  Scientists are developing new vaccines, but their effectiveness remains uncertain.

articles.title: RO systems should be maintained properly to be effective, says study - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: A recent study in Chennai, India, found that while reverse osmosis (RO) systems effectively remove microbes under ideal conditions, they are not a guarantee for safe drinking water. The study, published in the Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology, revealed that 31% of post-RO samples still contained Escherichia coli (E. coli), compared to 71% in untreated water.  The researchers found a correlation between education level and E. coli contamination, with higher levels of education associated with lower rates of contamination. The study emphasizes the need for proper maintenance and hygiene practices alongside reliable piped water supply and affordable servicing structures to ensure safe drinking water access.

articles.title: Melanoma skin cancer cases in UK hit record level, analysis finds | Skin cancer | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: Cancer Research UK has reported a record high of 20,980 melanoma cases in the UK for 2022, with projections suggesting that by 2040 there could be 26,500 new cases annually. The charity attributes the increase to the UK's growing and ageing population, and emphasizes that most cases are preventable through sun safety measures like seeking shade, covering up, and using sunscreen. Fiona Osgun, head of health information at Cancer Research UK, advises protecting skin from UV damage even on cooler or cloudier days. Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, stresses the importance of sensible sun exposure practices to prevent melanoma, urging individuals to seek medical attention if they notice any unusual changes in their skin.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo: Angry crowd sets Rwampara hospital tents on fire
articles.rephrased_article: An angry crowd in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo set fire to hospital tents used for Ebola isolation wards, after the death of a young man who was thought to have died from typhoid fever but whose body was not allowed to be buried. Luc Malembe Malembe, a local politician, witnessed the scene and stated that people did not believe the virus existed. The World Health Organization (WHO) has declared it a "public health emergency of international concern," but not at pandemic level.  The outbreak, caused by a rare species of Ebola known as Bundibugyo, has resulted in 139 deaths and two cases in neighboring Uganda.

articles.title: Qatar-based British-Pakistani scientist develops AI eye scan for early dementia diagnosis - World - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: Professor Rayaz Malik, a British-Pakistani scientist based in Qatar, has developed an AI-powered eye scan using corneal confocal microscopy (CCM) that can detect dementia and diabetic nerve damage years before symptoms appear.  This technology, traditionally used to diagnose infections and abnormalities in the front surface of the eye, has been shown to identify microscopic nerve fibre damage associated with diseases such as diabetes, chemotherapy, inflammatory disorders, and infectious diseases. Professor Malik believes this could be particularly important for countries facing ageing populations and rising rates of neurological disease.  The technology's ability to detect early-stage cognitive decline could lead to more effective treatments and earlier interventions.

articles.title: Bihar midday meal incident: HC asks whether NGO can continue providing meals - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: The Patna High Court has expressed concern over delays in the investigation of a midday meal incident where over 150 students fell ill in Saharsa district. The court questioned whether the NGO supplying meals to over 1,800 students should continue operations during the probe and raised concerns about discrepancies in food sample collection and testing.  The court directed officials to file affidavits explaining the processes involved. The matter will be heard again on June 2nd.

articles.title: Patient tests HIV-positive after surgery, triggering probe at Multan’s Nishtar Hospital - Pakistan - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: Nishtar Hospital in Multan, Pakistan, has formed a four-member inquiry committee to investigate allegations of medical negligence following a patient's surgery without mandatory HIV screening. The patient tested positive for the virus after the procedure and raised concerns among staff about potential exposure and lapses in infection control protocols.  The hospital claims that preventive measures were taken immediately, including disinfection of surgical instruments. Dr Riwad Noor, a member of the inquiry committee, stated they will submit their report within two days.

articles.title: Ebola: US ban on travellers from DRC, Uganda or South Sudan ‘not the solution’ | Global development | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organization (WHO) declared a public health emergency of international concern due to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with new cases reported in South Kivu province.  Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) criticized travel bans imposed by the US on citizens from the affected countries, arguing that they are ineffective and could exacerbate the situation. Dr Githinji Gitahi, CEO of Amref Health Africa, echoed this sentiment, emphasizing the need for investment in outbreak control at the source rather than isolating affected regions.  Uganda’s information minister, Chris Baryomunsi, countered by stating that his country has experience managing similar outbreaks and possesses the capacity to contain them.

articles.title: Autoimmune diseases higher than before; long-term effect of pesticides need to be studied: expert - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Sougata Bardhan, Associate Professor at Tennessee State University, is investigating the long-term effects of pesticides and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) on human health. His research, which focuses on the "One Health" concept, suggests that existing studies on short-term impacts may not reflect the full picture.  Dr. Bardhan is collaborating with Anirban Chakraborty, Director at Nitte University Centre for Science Education and Research, to study the effects of pesticides and GMOs on zebrafish, a model organism with a four-year life cycle that shares 70% of its genetic makeup with humans.  He emphasizes the importance of sustainable agricultural practices and the use of modern technology in managing food security while advocating for local produce consumption.

articles.title: Gonorrhoea and syphilis hit record levels in Europe, data shows
articles.rephrased_article: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) reported record levels of gonorrhoea and syphilis in Europe during 2024, with cases surging by 303% and over doubling respectively since 2015.  Bruno Ciancio, head of the agency's Directly Transmitted and Vaccine-Preventable Diseases unit, attributed the surge to widening gaps in testing and prevention efforts. The ECDC called for urgent action to address this public health crisis, emphasizing the potential for severe complications from these infections.

articles.title: Scientists turn sheep wool into a bone-healing material in a major medical breakthrough | - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: King's College London scientists have developed an experimental bone-healing material made from sheep wool that could offer a sustainable alternative to collagen. The research focused on keratin, a structural protein found in wool, hair, and nails. Laboratory and animal tests showed the wool-derived material successfully supported bone regeneration and produced tissue more closely resembling healthy natural bone than conventional collagen-based scaffolds. While further testing is needed before human trials, researchers believe this sustainable source of biomaterials could revolutionize bone repair and dental reconstruction.

articles.title: New Mexico Substance Exposure: Mystery substance scare in New Mexico: 3 dead, first responders quarantined over toxic exposure - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: Three people died and over a dozen first responders were exposed to an unidentified substance at a rural home in New Mexico. Mountainair Mayor Peter Nieto stated that authorities are investigating the substance's nature, ruling out carbon monoxide and natural gas but not yet identifying it.  The incident prompted several firefighters and EMTs to experience symptoms like nausea, vomiting, and dizziness after contact with the substance. University of New Mexico Hospital officials assessed 23 exposed individuals, most of whom were first responders who showed no symptoms. While authorities believe the substance may be transmitted through contact and not airborne, the investigation continues.

articles.title: Canada faces calls for investigation into death of woman after plasma donation | Canada | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: Patient advocates are calling for a new investigation into the death of Rodiyat Alabede, a young woman who died after donating plasma in Winnipeg.  Health Canada initially found no link between her death and the donation, but campaigners allege significant discrepancies between the autopsy report and the agency's medical summary. Grifols, the company that operated the facility where Alabede donated, has acknowledged issues with staff training and reporting, but maintains it is working to address them.  The advocacy group representing Alabede's family is demanding a reopened investigation and the suspension of Grifols' license pending further review.

articles.title: ‘Research here is world class’: son of Steve Jobs looks to invest in UK cancer care | Venture capital | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: Reed Jobs, a venture capitalist and the son of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, is leading an oncology-focused venture capital fund called Yosemite, which has invested in over 20 healthcare startups.  The firm focuses on gene therapy, cancer vaccines, radiopharmaceuticals, and artificial intelligence, with a goal of making cancer treatable and non-lethal. Yosemite receives funding from organizations like LifeArc, a UK-based not-for-profit focused on rare diseases, and has partnerships with universities like Oxford and Cambridge.  Jobs hopes to see a shift in cancer care towards early diagnosis and personalized treatment similar to advances made with HIV and cardiovascular disease.

articles.title: ASHAs meet Kerala CM-designate V.D. Satheesan, urge him to honour pre-poll promises - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Kerala ASHA Health Workers’ Association (KAHWA) met with V.D. Satheesan, the new Chief Minister-designate, to reiterate their demands for an increase in honorarium and retirement benefits. They expressed hope that the new government would prioritize addressing their concerns.  Satheesan assured them that he would not forget his pre-election promise of resolving their grievances.

articles.title: ‘Within hours, he was gone’: Berkshire father shares pain after son dies in meningitis outbreak
articles.rephrased_article: Lewis Waters, a 17-year-old student at The Henley College, tragically died from sepsis after contracting meningitis. His father, Sean Waters, described his son as "funny, sociable, kind-hearted" and deeply devoted to his family and friends. Two other students in Berkshire are also being treated for meningitis, prompting concerns about the disease's rapid progression and a call for wider vaccination programs among young adults. The UK Health Security Agency is investigating the cases and offering antibiotics to close contacts as a precautionary measure.

articles.title: FDA turmoil deepens as top drug chief departs claiming she was fired | US news | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) experienced a series of high-profile departures this week, including the acting drug chief, Tracy Beth Høeg, and the acting vaccines chief, Katherine Szarama. Marty Makary, who resigned on Tuesday, has been replaced by Kyle Diamantas as acting commissioner, while Michael Davis will serve as acting director of the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER).  The departures come amid controversy surrounding FDA decisions on vaccines, rare disease medications, staff layoffs, and low morale.

articles.title: What is a 'safe death'? Mentally ill woman asks for assisted dying in Canada
articles.rephrased_article: Claire Brosseau, a 49-year-old woman with debilitating mental illness from bipolar disorder and PTSD, is seeking medically assisted dying (MAID) in Canada.  She argues that current laws are exclusionary to those with mental illness and unconstitutional. Prime Minister Mark Carney is awaiting a report from a parliamentary committee reviewing the expansion of MAID to include patients with severe, treatment-resistant mental illness. The committee has faced criticism for its composition and process, with Brosseau expressing concerns about being excluded from testifying.  The Canadian government's response to her legal challenge remains pending.

articles.title: Meningitis outbreak sparks alarm after student dies and 2 others fall ill in Reading Area
articles.rephrased_article: UKHSA officials are investigating a meningitis outbreak in the Reading and Oxfordshire area after one student's death and two hospitalizations. The Henley College student who died, Lewis Waters, was found to have tested positive for MenB.  Authorities are working with schools and families, offering precautionary antibiotics to prevent further spread. Public health officials are urging parents, students, and schools to stay alert for symptoms such as high fever, headache, vomiting, and stiff neck, which can appear in any order and worsen rapidly. The UKHSA has reassured the public that large outbreaks remain rare but acknowledges recent clusters have raised concerns about meningitis transmission among young people.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo: Over 80 dead, 246 cases reported in Ituri province; health emergency declared
articles.rephrased_article: Africa CDC has declared an Ebola outbreak in the eastern Ituri province of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with 246 cases and 80 deaths reported. The virus, confirmed in 13 of 20 samples, is believed to have originated in bats and spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids. Health officials warn of a high risk of further spread due to population movement and mining activity. Africa CDC has called for joint action with neighboring countries to strengthen surveillance and response measures.

articles.title: Joyride horse dies of highly contagious zoonotic disease disease in Chennai; Tamil Nadu goes into alert mode - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: The ICAR–National Research Centre on Equines (NRCE) confirmed that a horse used for joyrides in the city has died from glanders, a highly contagious bacterial disease affecting equines. The Besant Memorial Animal Dispensary (BMAD) alerted authorities after noticing the horse's weakened condition and sent samples to the NRCE for testing. The NRCE advised the Tamil Nadu Animal Husbandry Department to isolate and monitor all equines in the area, implement surveillance and testing protocols, and regulate inter-state movement of horses. The Tamil Nadu Animal Welfare Board has requested that samples be collected from all joyride horses.

articles.title: WHO confirms 10 global hantavirus cases, Hondius crew remain symptom-free | World Health Organization News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organization (WHO) confirmed 10 global hantavirus cases, lowering its previous count of 11.  Maria Van Kerkhove, the WHO's director for epidemic and pandemic preparedness and prevention, stated that the risk to the global population is low. The outbreak began on a Dutch luxury cruise ship, the MV Hondius, which departed Argentina for a polar expedition.  The captain and crew remain onboard and are being monitored; however, three passengers have died since the outbreak began. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, confirmed that more cases may be reported in coming days as passengers return to their countries.

articles.title: Hantavirus outbreak tests post-Covid health communications playbook - World - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: A mid-ocean cruise ship in quarantine, the MV Hondius, has sparked renewed concern about hantavirus after several deaths and illnesses. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with other health organizations like the World Health Organization (WHO), are working to communicate clearly about the virus's low risk while addressing misinformation and public anxiety.  Experts emphasize that lessons learned from the COVID-19 pandemic should be applied to ensure effective communication and mitigate fear surrounding hantavirus.

articles.title: Meningitis outbreak in Berkshire causes panic in three schools
articles.rephrased_article: The UK Health Security Agency confirmed a student death from meningococcal meningitis at Henley College, with two other Berkshire schools, Reading Blue Coat School and Highdown Secondary School and Sixth Form Centre, also affected.  Dr Rachel Mearkle, of the UKHSA, assured the public that while cases are rare, close contact is necessary for transmission and precautionary measures are being taken.  The outbreak is not linked to the Kent meningitis B strain but is a different strain.

articles.title: Hantavirus: how scared should we be? | News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: Three people have died after a hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship, prompting global concern and echoing the anxieties surrounding COVID-19.  Experts emphasize that the virus is different but acknowledge the impact of the pandemic on public trust.

articles.title: Health officials raise alarm over new Ebola outbreak in DR Congo | News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported 246 suspected Ebola cases and 65 deaths in the Ituri province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The outbreak, which comes five months after the previous one was declared over, is raising concerns about its potential spread due to poor security and population movement. The DRC government faces challenges controlling the virus, particularly in a remote region with limited road networks.  The CDC, along with health authorities from Uganda and South Sudan, will convene an urgent meeting to address immediate response priorities, including cross-border coordination, surveillance, and resource mobilization.

articles.title: CS wants officials to expedite works ahead of launch of digital health cards on June 2 - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Chief Secretary K. Ramakrishna Rao directed officials to expedite the launch of digital health cards for employees on June 2nd, coinciding with the State formation day. During a Joint Staff Council meeting, Rao addressed employee grievances related to the Pay Revision Commission report, pending bills, and transfers under GO 317. He assured employees that the government would address the PRC report promptly and encouraged unions to utilize technology for efficient problem resolution.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak kills 65 people in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo | Global development | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) reported that an outbreak of Ebola has killed 65 people in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with 246 suspected cases. The outbreak is occurring in Ituri province, a region bordering Uganda and South Sudan, where movement between areas makes disease control difficult.  Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of Africa CDC, stated that rapid regional coordination is essential given the high population movement between affected areas and neighboring countries.

articles.title: US Supreme Court restores access to abortion pill mifepristone for now
articles.rephrased_article: The US Supreme Court has issued a stay that allows the abortion pill, mifepristone, to continue being accessed by mail.  This decision comes after lower courts placed significant restrictions on access to the drug as part of an ongoing lawsuit. The ruling will remain in place until the justices decide whether to hear the manufacturers' case. Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, the most conservative justices, dissented from the decision.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak kills 65 in eastern DR Congo's Ituri province
articles.rephrased_article: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC Africa) has declared an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ituri province, following reports of 246 cases and 65 deaths. The virus is believed to have spread from bats and is spreading through direct contact with bodily fluids. The Congolese government has not yet officially declared an outbreak but is expected to do so later on Friday.  Preliminary tests conducted at the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB) in Kinshasa have detected the virus in 13 of 20 samples analyzed.

articles.title: Effluent discharge into canal suspected to have triggered hepatitis A outbreak - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Kothamangalam municipality is facing a hepatitis A outbreak after water contamination from effluent pipes in the Muvattupuzha minor irrigation project was linked to the spread of the disease. Health authorities have reported 37 cases, with the first case identified on March 29 and the last on April 24. The municipality has initiated measures such as cleaning the canal, chlorinating wells, and installing cautionary notices to contain the outbreak.  The region will be declared disease-free only after 90 days without new cases.

articles.title: Supreme court allows abortion pill mifepristone to continue to be available by mail | US supreme court | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The US Supreme Court overturned a decision by the Fifth Circuit that had banned nationwide access to mail-order mifepristone. The court ruled 7-2, ending a ban on the medication and allowing it to be shipped to patients across the country. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented, with Thomas calling the mailing of mifepristone "criminal enterprise" and Alito arguing that the Comstock Act should apply to the drug.  The case is expected to return to the Fifth Circuit for further proceedings.

articles.title: One dead and two more ill after meningitis outbreak in Berkshire | Meningitis | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) confirmed new cases of meningococcal meningitis in Reading, resulting in the death of a student and two others being treated.  While officials emphasized that large outbreaks are rare, they are working with partners to provide public health advice and antibiotics to close contacts. The UKHSA also reminded the public that anyone can contract meningitis and urged individuals to seek medical attention if experiencing any concerning symptoms.

articles.title: Why a Bill Gates-backed insect factory releases 30 million mosquitoes every week
articles.rephrased_article: Scientists at a mosquito breeding facility in Medellín, Colombia, are releasing millions of mosquitoes carrying a harmless bacteria called Wolbachia into the environment. This project, backed by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, aims to reduce the spread of diseases like dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and yellow fever by replacing disease-carrying mosquitoes with less harmful ones. The program has shown promising results in reducing dengue infections in Indonesia and Colombia.  The goal is not to eliminate mosquitoes but to gradually replace dangerous mosquito populations with less harmful ones.

articles.title: France, Netherlands say all hantavirus contact cases negative - World - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: France’s health minister announced that all close contacts of a hantavirus case linked to the MV Hondius cruise ship have tested negative. Dutch authorities confirmed that all evacuees from the ship in the Netherlands also tested negative.  The 26 individuals in France, including 22 identified as close contacts of a Dutch woman who died in South Africa, are being monitored for hantavirus. The European Union will enhance information sharing to combat hantavirus. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is actively monitoring the situation and conducting public health assessments in Nebraska where 16 passengers from the ship have been quarantined.

articles.title: NDIS cuts could leave some participants with a funding gap. How will the changes affect you? | Disability | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: Mark Butler, Australian health minister, has proposed significant changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS). The legislation aims to reduce overall funding for support categories, determine pricing guides and caps for services and support, and grant the minister sweeping powers over NDIS rules. The bill also clarifies eligibility criteria, including a focus on "substantially reduced functional capacity" and exhaustion of "all appropriate" treatment options.  The changes are part of a plan to save $36.2 billion over four years, with potential for funding gaps for some participants. The legislation is currently under scrutiny by parliament and will undergo public hearings before final implementation.

articles.title: Hantavirus outbreak: Deadly Andes strain detected in cruise ship cases; eight cases confirmed - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organisation (WHO) reported eight confirmed cases of Andes virus infection among the passengers and crew of the cruise ship MV Hondius, with three deaths linked to the outbreak.  Two deceased individuals had confirmed Andes virus infections, while the third was classified as a probable case. The WHO stated that the public health risk remains moderate for those who were on board but low for the rest of the world. The American passenger involved in an inconclusive case is currently asymptomatic and undergoing further testing after initial positive and negative results.  Dr Stephen Kornfeld, an oncologist, was placed in a biocontainment unit at the University of Nebraska Medical Center after an inconclusive nasal swab result but has since been cleared to leave quarantine.

articles.title: Australians from hantavirus cruise ship to fly out of Netherlands in full PPE after plane and crew secured | Hantavirus | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: Australian citizens and a New Zealand citizen aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which is currently in the Netherlands, will be returning home after a complex international effort.  The Australian government secured an aircraft and crew for their safe transport from the Netherlands to Perth, where they will undergo a three-week quarantine at Bullsbrook facility. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade worked with national and international partners to ensure the safe return of all passengers and crew members. The outbreak has now reached 11 reported cases, with nine confirmed, and has resulted in three deaths.  The World Health Organization maintains that the threat to the general public remains low but urges caution as the virus can be serious.

articles.title: Hantavirus: After hantavirus, now norovirus? How a gut bug forced a France cruise ship into lockdown - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: French authorities lifted restrictions on the British cruise ship Ambition, after tests confirmed a gastrointestinal virus, likely norovirus, was behind an outbreak that sickened dozens of passengers. The ship, operated by Ambassador Cruise Line, had been placed under temporary lockdown in Bordeaux following concerns over a possible link to a hantavirus outbreak aboard another vessel. While the outbreak initially raised global concern due to the recent hantavirus case on the Dutch-flagged MV Hondius, health officials stated there was “no reason” to connect the two incidents.  The ship's passengers were largely from Britain and Ireland, with 1,233 people onboard.

articles.title: NHS drugs go-ahead offers lifeline to children with rare muscle-wasting disease | Children | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) has published final draft guidance recommending that any patient with spinal muscular atrophy can receive either nusinersen or risdiplam from the NHS. Prof James Palmer, NHS England’s national medical director for specialized services, stated that these treatments offer a "phenomenal step forward" in care for children and families affected by SMA.  The drugs have been available in a limited way since 2019 and 2021 respectively. Portia Thorman, whose nine-year-old son Ezra received nusinersen, said the drug has transformed his life, allowing him to attend primary school. The NHS plans to start an "in-service evaluation" of newborn screening for SMA in October, which may pave the way for it to become part of routine care.

articles.title: JD Vance threatens health funding to states that don’t comply with White House anti-fraud effort | US healthcare | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: JD Vance, the US vice-president, threatened to withhold federal funding for government health insurance programs in states that fail to comply with a crackdown on suspected fraud. CMS, the agency responsible for Medicaid and Medicare, announced a six-month halt on new Medicare enrollment for hospices and home health agencies while investigating potential fraud alongside Vance's taskforce.  The administration will review anti-fraud funding for states deemed non-compliant, but it is unclear how extensive these actions will be or what impact they will have on access to care.

articles.title: Drug overdose deaths drop in United States for third year in a row | Drugs News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released data showing a nearly 14 percent decline in drug overdose deaths in 2025, reaching nearly 70,000. This marks the third consecutive year of declining overdose deaths, attributed to factors such as increased availability of naloxone, fentanyl testing strips, and regulatory changes in China limiting access to fentanyl-making chemicals. While the trend is positive, seven states saw increases in overdose deaths.  President Donald Trump's administration has highlighted the decrease as a sign of success for its crackdown on drug trafficking, while experts have criticized such claims as exaggerated.

articles.title: 'No indication' Andes strain of hantavirus has mutated: EU agency - World - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) stated that there is no evidence suggesting the Andes strain of hantavirus has mutated following a deadly outbreak on a cruise ship. Andreas Hoefer, a microbiologist from the ECDC, explained preliminary genome sequencing data indicates a single transmission event from an infected animal to humans.  The World Health Organisation (WHO) recommends a 42-day quarantine and constant monitoring for high-risk contacts due to the long incubation period of six weeks.

articles.title: Pakistan, WHO launch Prime Minister's Hepatitis C Elimination Programme - Pakistan - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: Pakistan and the World Health Organization (WHO) launched the Prime Minister’s Hepatitis C Elimination Programme in Islamabad. The program aims to eliminate hepatitis C as a public health threat by 2030, with an initial focus on screening and treatment for 1.6 million people over six months.  The initiative will provide free three-to-six month treatment courses for all patients. Federal Health Minister Mustafa Kamal emphasized the importance of prevention and early intervention in combating the disease, which affects nearly 10 million Pakistanis. The program is supported by the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) to ensure nationwide screening using national database integration.

articles.title: Woman isolating on British island in South Pacific after hantavirus contact
articles.rephrased_article: A woman who traveled on a hantavirus-hit cruise ship is currently isolating on the Pitcairn Islands after contact with an infected individual. The UK foreign office and UKHSA are coordinating with local authorities to manage risks, while the WHO has confirmed nine cases of the virus, including two suspected.  The woman's isolation is expected to last 45 days as a precaution, but she will not be allowed to re-enter French Polynesia due to potential risk to others. The French Polynesian government stated that passengers on the same flight from San Francisco to Tahiti are not considered close contacts and the risk of infection is low.

articles.title: France confines over 1,700 passengers on cruise ship over gastroenteritis | Health News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: French authorities have temporarily restricted the disembarkation of 1,233 passengers and 514 crew members on a British cruise ship docked in Bordeaux after nearly 50 suspected cases of gastroenteritis were reported. The Ambition, carrying mostly British or Irish nationals, had travelled from Belfast and Liverpool before arriving in southwestern France on Tuesday evening. Cruise operator Ambassador Cruise Line has introduced enhanced sanitation measures and offered full refunds to affected passengers. Health officials are conducting medical tests to determine the cause of the outbreak, which is not believed to be linked to a hantavirus cluster reported on another ship.

articles.title: More than 1,000 passengers held on cruise after gastrointestinal illness outbreak
articles.rephrased_article: Ambassador Cruise Line is operating a UK-operated cruise ship, the Ambition, in France after 49 passengers fell ill with gastrointestinal illness. Local health authorities have suspended passenger disembarkations and dispatched a medical team to assess the situation.  The cruise line has implemented enhanced sanitation protocols and reported that 48 passengers and one crew member are displaying symptoms consistent with gastrointestinal illness. The cause of death for a 92-year-old man who passed away on board is yet to be determined.

articles.title: Hantavirus outbreak: Passengers evacuated from cruise ship to leave hospital after 72-hour quarantine - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: Passengers evacuated from the virus-hit Dutch cruise ship MV Hondius are set to begin leaving a specialist isolation facility in the UK after completing an initial 72-hour quarantine period.  All passengers remain healthy and asymptomatic, but will continue self-isolation at home for another 42 days as a precaution. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) stated that public health specialists will assess whether individuals can safely isolate at home or if alternative accommodation arrangements are necessary. The outbreak aboard the expedition cruise ship has so far been linked to three deaths, including two confirmed hantavirus cases.  The WHO has confirmed six infections linked to the outbreak, with more potential cases still possible.

articles.title: The class politics of modern outbreaks | Health | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: A recent hantavirus outbreak on the MV Hondius, a luxury cruise ship, highlights concerns about elite mobility and its impact on global health. The outbreak, which has led to confirmed cases and deaths, underscores the unequal distribution of risks associated with disease transmission during pandemics.  While wealthy passengers often travel freely and experience minimal consequences, poorer populations in regions where outbreaks occur bear the brunt of the risk. This pattern reflects a larger issue of inequality within globalization, where wealthier individuals contribute disproportionately to the spread of diseases while those with fewer resources are most vulnerable to their effects.

articles.title: London prisoner with muscle-wasting condition claims he has to crawl on floor | UK news | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: Umer Khalid, a prisoner at Wormwood Scrubs awaiting trial for alleged involvement in a break-in at RAF Brize Norton, claims he has been forced to crawl due to inadequate medical care and lack of a wheelchair. Khalid, who suffers from limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, alleges that prison officials have ignored his needs, including missed appointments with healthcare professionals and insufficient access to medication and high protein food. He also claims to have been left in his cell during a fire alarm evacuation and denied proper treatment for his condition despite being diagnosed with muscular dystrophy in 2014. Shabana Khalid, his mother, expressed outrage at the prison's response, stating that her son is suffering from severe physical deterioration.

articles.title: Inquest into death of Clare Nowland after Tasering by NSW police aims to answer ‘outstanding questions’ | New South Wales | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: An inquest into the death of 95-year-old Clare Nowland, who died after being Tasered by Constable Kristian James Samuel White at Yallambee Lodge nursing home in Cooma, is expected to focus on improving training for first responders dealing with aggressive dementia patients. The three-day inquest will examine systemic issues related to dementia care and training for aged care staff, police, and ambulance officers, as well as the communication between these groups.  State coroner Teresa O’Sullivan will examine whether Nowland's care was reasonable and if there were any contributing factors that led to her death.

articles.title: Free vaccination for cervical cancer until May 31 - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: District Collector G. Priyanka announced the final phase of the HPV vaccination campaign against cervical cancer in the district, urging all eligible girls to receive the vaccine before May 31, 2026.  The campaign aims to vaccinate a total of 22,358 girls aged 14 and under, with only 34% currently vaccinated as of the current date. The vaccination facility will cease operation after this deadline.

articles.title: Older people risk mental decline if they do long hours of caring, UK study shows | Carers | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: Carers UK and researchers at University College London have found that providing care for 5 to 9 hours a week can boost brain health, while long hours of care lead to accelerated cognitive decline. The study compared the cognitive health of 2,765 carers aged 50 or over with 2,765 non-carers and found that those providing more than 50 hours of care experienced faster mental decline.  The researchers suggest that the government should provide more support for "intensive" carers through better access to funded formal and replacement care. The findings highlight the need for increased support for family caregivers who often face significant stress and burnout.

articles.title: Metal screw removed from baby’s lung at Government Chengalpattu Medical College Hospital - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Doctors at the Government Chengalpattu Medical College Hospital successfully removed a small metal screw from the right lung of a one-year-old girl who presented with breathing difficulties. The procedure, performed by a team led by associate professor of paediatrics Sarath Balaji, involved a minimally invasive bronchoscope and forceps. The child has since recovered and is doing well.

articles.title: WHO chief says 'work not over' after hantavirus evacuation - World - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus stated that the global public health risk from the hantavirus outbreak on the cruise ship MV Hondius is low, but the situation could change.  He emphasized the need for continued monitoring and highlighted the importance of following WHO guidelines, including quarantine measures. While some countries adopted different approaches to handling returning evacuees, WHO officials urged adherence to their recommendations.

articles.title: Capacity of lifts not kept up with UK obesity levels, study shows | Obesity | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: Researchers have found that lifts in the UK and mainland Europe are no longer large enough to accommodate the increasing weight of adults, raising concerns about safety and equity. A study presented at the European Congress on Obesity found that maximum lift capacities haven't increased since around 2004 despite average adult weights rising significantly. The research suggests manufacturers have focused on floor space rather than weight, failing to account for the increase in obesity rates. Prof Nick Finer, president of the International Prader-Willi Syndrome Organisation and lead author of the study, emphasized that this issue impacts not only safety but also social inclusion by creating stigma for individuals with obesity.

articles.title: Pakistan to face growing health risk as international funding to health sector continues to decline: report - Pakistan - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: Pakistan faces serious health risks due to declining international funding for its healthcare sector.  A report by the think tank Tabadlab warns that cuts in Official Development Assistance (ODA) could lead to disruptions in disease control programs, immunisation efforts, and institutional capacity across the country. The report highlights a sharp decline in global ODA flows since 2019, with total funding dropping from $215 billion in 2024 to $174.3 billion in 2025.  The report emphasizes the need for Pakistan to reduce its reliance on external health financing and strengthen domestic systems before further aid cuts worsen the situation. The report recommends establishing a National Health Financing Forum, creating an ODA registry, introducing a health financing risk matrix, and reforming governance structures within the healthcare sector.

articles.title: French minister says uncertain if hantavirus strain from cruise ship has mutated - World - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: French Health Minister Stephanie Rist stated that the hantavirus strain on the MV Hondius cruise ship may have mutated, but officials remain "rather reassured" due to a lack of complete sequencing data. The outbreak has been linked to the Andes strain of hantavirus and is being investigated by World Health Organisation, which confirmed nine cases and urged isolation of suspected individuals. Italy's top infectious diseases hospital will examine biological samples from a man in quarantine who came into contact with a woman who died from the virus, but no further details were provided.

articles.title: WHO head tells countries to prepare for more hantavirus cases | Hantavirus | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organization (WHO) has urged countries to prepare for more hantavirus cases following the outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship. The virus, which can be transmitted person-to-person in rare cases, has been confirmed in nine individuals, including a French woman and a US national who were evacuated from the ship. Spain played a crucial role in evacuating over 120 passengers and crew members, receiving praise from the WHO for its compassion and solidarity.  The UK is also preparing to bring 10 people from remote South Atlantic islands into the country for precautionary isolation. The WHO has acknowledged that more cases are likely due to interactions on board before preventative measures were taken.

articles.title: ‘Unprecedented’ global effort gives new name to polycystic ovary syndrome – and new hope to millions of women | Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: After a decade of collaboration, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) has been renamed to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). The new name reflects the condition's broader impact on multiple systems in the body, including metabolism and risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease.  The renaming was spearheaded by endocrinologist Prof Helena Teede, who emphasized that the term "polycystic" contributed to delayed diagnosis and inadequate medical care. Patients advocated for the change, highlighting the need for a name that better reflects the condition's complexity. The new name will be implemented in international guidelines for managing PCOS, with full implementation planned for 2028.

articles.title: No sign of larger hantavirus outbreak, says UN health agency
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organization (WHO) has stated that there is "no sign" of a larger hantavirus outbreak after the evacuation of the last passengers from the disease-stricken cruise ship, MV Hondius.  Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, head of the WHO, warned that the situation could change and more cases might emerge in the coming weeks. The ship is expected to arrive in Rotterdam on May 17th after a six-day voyage.  The final six passengers, including crew members from various countries, have been repatriated to their home countries.

articles.title: Last passengers from hantavirus-hit ship evacuated; American tests positive | Health News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced that one of the 18 American passengers evacuated from the hantavirus-stricken cruise ship, MV Hondius, has tested positive for the respiratory infection. The last two evacuation flights carrying passengers and crew from the ship landed in the Netherlands, where the vessel will undergo disinfection.  The World Health Organization (WHO) maintains that the risk to the public remains low, but recommends a 42-day quarantine for all passengers.

articles.title: Quest for a rare bird, a landfill visit, a deadly outbreak: How Leo Schilperoord became hantavirus 'patient zero' - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: Leo Schilperoord, a Dutch ornithologist, is confirmed as the patient zero in a deadly hantavirus outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship. Authorities suspect he contracted the virus from long-tailed pygmy rice rats carrying the Andes strain of hantavirus while birdwatching at a landfill outside Ushuaia, Argentina.  The couple's travels across South America and Sri Lanka prior to their arrival on the ship are believed to have exposed them to the virus. Mirjam Schilperoord, his wife, also died after experiencing symptoms of the illness during her journey. The outbreak led to the evacuation of passengers and crew from the ship, with 94 people repatriated to their home countries.

articles.title: Arts and cultural engagement ‘linked to slower pace of biological ageing’ | Ageing | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: A new study published in the journal Innovation in Aging found that participating in artistic activities, such as singing, painting, or attending art exhibitions, can slow biological aging. Prof Daisy Fancourt, head of the social biobehavioral research group at University College London, and her colleagues analyzed data from 3,556 adults in the UK Household Longitudinal Study, finding those who engaged in arts activities weekly slowed their biological aging by an average of 4%, while monthly engagement led to a slowdown of 3%. The study suggests that engaging with art can have similar benefits to exercise on slowing down biological aging. Arts Council England director Hollie Smith-Charles believes these findings emphasize the importance of access to culture for overall well-being and longevity.

articles.title: US, French nationals from hantavirus ship test positive - World - DAWN.COM
articles.rephrased_article: The World Health Organization (WHO) and Spanish health officials are overseeing the repatriation of passengers from the cruise ship, MV Hondius, which was hit by a deadly hantavirus outbreak.  Two passengers from the ship have tested positive for the Andes virus, with one American national experiencing mild symptoms. The operation to evacuate nearly 150 passengers and crew members is ongoing, with most expected to be flown to their respective countries by Monday afternoon. WHO officials are recommending a 42-day quarantine and active follow-up, but some passengers may choose to return home without further isolation depending on the risk assessment.

articles.title: Most drowning cases occur in summer: Fire dept. - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Fire and Rescue Services department reported a surge in drowning cases involving students during summer vacation.  Three dental students from Baselios Dental College drowned in the Palavan river near Kothamangalam, while another student drowned in a quarry in Thrikkariyoor panchayat. The incidents highlight the dangers of strong undercurrents and deep pits in the picturesque but treacherous river. To address this issue, Kothamangalam fire station organized a 10-day swimming camp for students.

articles.title: Evacuated US and French MV Hondius passengers test positive for hantavirus | Hantavirus | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: A French woman and an American passenger evacuated from the cruise ship MV Hondius, which was at the center of a deadly hantavirus outbreak, have tested positive for the virus.  Stéphanie Rist, French health minister, confirmed that the French woman is in serious condition and being treated in Paris. The US health department announced that one American national evacuated from the ship has tested positive for the Andes strain of hantavirus, while another passenger had mild symptoms.  The repatriation operation to evacuate over 100 people from 23 nationalities continued on Monday with more than 94 passengers already flown out. Maud Bregeon, a French government spokesperson, stated that the risk for global public health is low and authorities are taking necessary measures to protect the French people.

articles.title: US cruise ship passengers being monitored for hantavirus in Nebraska
articles.rephrased_article: US passengers evacuated from a cruise ship in the Canary Islands are being monitored for hantavirus exposure. Admiral Brian Christine, of the US Health and Human Services department (HHS), stated that the risk to the public is very low, as the Andes variant does not easily spread.  The 16 passengers quarantined at Nebraska's national quarantine unit are in good spirits and will undergo further assessment before determining if they need to complete the full 42-day quarantine period.

articles.title: Where did the hantavirus outbreak start, and where has it spread? | Health News | Al Jazeera
articles.rephrased_article: The hantavirus outbreak began on the MV Hondius cruise ship, which departed from Argentina on April 1. The virus has spread to at least 20 countries with passengers being evacuated and quarantined in various locations. At least three people have died, including an elderly Dutch couple who were among the first to develop symptoms.  The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends testing and monitoring for at least 42 days after suspected exposure. The outbreak is linked to the Andes strain of hantavirus, which is endemic in rural parts of South America.

articles.title: Govt. to bring reforms in AYUSH sector to enhance quality: Health Minister - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: The State government of Andhra Pradesh is implementing reforms in the AYUSH sector to enhance healthcare services and combat the distribution of fake drugs. Minister for Health, Medical Education and Family Welfare Satya Kumar Yadav announced the establishment of three committees – an expert committee, a stakeholders committee, and a technical committee – to develop new guidelines. The committees will consult experts, gather public feedback, and study best practices from other states like Kerala, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu before submitting their recommendations.  The aim is to strengthen the regulatory framework for AYUSH clinics and hospitals, ensuring all practitioners are qualified and services meet national standards.

articles.title: US and French nationals test positive for hantavirus after leaving ship
articles.rephrased_article: US and French nationals who recently left a cruise ship with a deadly hantavirus outbreak have tested positive for the virus.  The US Department of Health and Human Services said all 17 US citizens on the repatriation flight will undergo clinical assessment at a medical facility in Nebraska, while seven other US passengers are being monitored in their home states. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended 42 days of isolation for those leaving the ship, but the US Centers for Disease Control (CDC) has stated that human-to-human transmission is rare and it should not be treated like the Covid virus.

articles.title: Experts call for UK four-day week as study links long work hours to obesity | Obesity | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: International research, presented at the European Congress on Obesity, found a correlation between longer working hours and higher obesity rates in 33 OECD countries.  The study suggests that reducing annual working hours by 1% could decrease obesity rates by 0.16%. Dr Pradeepa Korale-Gedara, of the University of Queensland, Australia, attributes this to increased stress levels from long work hours leading to fat storage and a lack of time for exercise. While researchers acknowledge the need for further investigation, experts advocate for a four-day work week as a potential solution to combat obesity in the UK.

articles.title: ‘Not like Covid’: Indian-American scientist says there is no need to panic over Hantavirus in US - The Times of India
articles.rephrased_article: Jay Bhattacharya, acting US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Director, addressed concerns about a hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship near Spain's Canary Islands. He stated the situation is not COVID-19 and that existing protocols have been successful in containing past outbreaks.  The outbreak has resulted in three deaths and five serious illnesses among passengers aboard the MV 'Hondius', with 17 Americans reportedly onboard. The CDC is monitoring the situation, offering quarantine options for those returning to the US, and following a similar strategy used during the 2018 Andes hantavirus outbreak.

articles.title: Iranian activist tells BBC how fear of war restarting intensifies trauma of repression
articles.rephrased_article: Shirin, an Iranian activist, is experiencing severe anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder due to the ongoing war and regime repression.  She has been subjected to multiple arrests and interrogations by secret police, leading to physical injury and psychological trauma. Human Rights Watch (HRW) reports that detainees are facing human rights violations and even death, while Iranian Red Crescent receives thousands of calls for mental health support. The combination of state repression and the US-Israeli bombing campaign has intensified Iran's already profound mental health crisis.

articles.title: Apollo Hospitals launches centre for venous disorders - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Apollo Hospitals has opened a Centre for Venous Disorders at its Greams Road hospital in Chennai. The centre, focusing on conditions like varicose veins and deep vein thrombosis, aims to provide comprehensive treatment through specialized care from vascular surgeons, radiologists, dermatologists, and wound care specialists.  The launch was attended by Ilankumaran Kaliamoorthy, CEO of the Chennai Region, along with vascular surgeons Balaji and Rajarajan Venkatesan and Naveen, CEO of Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road.

articles.title: French national from hantavirus cruise ship shows symptoms during airlift
articles.rephrased_article: Sebastian Lecornu, the French prime minister, announced that a French national on a chartered flight from Tenerife to Paris showed symptoms of hantavirus after returning from the cruise ship MV Hondius.  All five passengers evacuated from the vessel have been placed in strict isolation until further notice. The WHO and Spanish Health Secretary Javier Padilla coordinated the repatriation process, which saw over 90 passengers and crew flown home to various destinations including France, Spain, the UK, Australia, and the Netherlands. British nationals arriving back in the UK will be quarantined for up to 72 hours before being assessed for further isolation.

articles.title: Tripura pharmacists to join strike on May 20 - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: The All India Organisation of Chemists and Druggists is calling for a strike on May 20th, affecting health services in Tripura. The strike demands the cessation of online medicine sales, corporate-run industry deep discounts, and the halt of spurious medication sales.  The Tripura Chemists and Druggists Association, affiliated with the national body, will join the strike, resulting in approximately 3,000 pharmacies remaining closed. The State Health and Family Welfare Department and the State Drug Control Authority are reportedly taking steps to mitigate the impact of the strike.

articles.title: Kochi Port on alert after hantavirus outbreak on cruise ship - The Hindu
articles.rephrased_article: Kochi Port authorities are maintaining heightened vigilance following the deaths linked to hantavirus infection aboard a Dutch cruise ship, MV Hondius.  The outbreak of the Andes virus strain has been contained within the vessel and no national-level guidelines or advisories have been issued. The port is currently monitoring passengers and crew arriving at the port with a risk-based approach, requiring health declarations and initiating appropriate measures if symptoms are suspected.

articles.title: British paratroopers land on Tristan da Cunha for suspected hantavirus case | Hantavirus | The Guardian
articles.rephrased_article: The UK Health Security Agency confirmed a suspected hantavirus case on the remote island of Tristan da Cunha, prompting the Ministry of Defence to deploy six paratroopers and medical supplies via parachute. articles.title: Why is being a mother so expensive in the United States? | Infographic News | Al Jazeera

articles.title: This is the sentence that protects every abuser in Pakistan - Pakistan - DAWN.COM
